dialogs.title: စကားပြော — Arranging lunch

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: Clock times are built as **number + နာရီ**, with the minutes added after. နာရီ (*na-yee*) means both "hour, o'clock" and "watch", and comes from Sanskrit.

head: English
Burmese
Say it
rows: ဘယ်နှစ်နာရီလဲ
သုံးနာရီ ဆယ်မိနစ်
သုံးနာရီ ဆယ့်ငါးမိနစ်
သုံးနာရီ ထိုးဖို့ ဆယ်မိနစ်
သုံးနာရီတိတိ

after: ⚠️ For **minutes to the hour**, Burmese uses ထိုးဖို့ (*htoh:-hpoh.*, "to strike") — literally "ten minutes for three to strike". In fast speech it's often shortened, and beginners can avoid it by giving the minutes past instead.

grammars.title: ⚠️ ခွဲ — the half hour points BACK
body: English speakers are in luck here: Burmese works like "half past". But if you know German, Dutch, or another language where "half three" means 2:30, this trap can cost you an appointment.

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
In English
rows: နှစ်နာရီခွဲ
ဆယ့်တစ်နာရီခွဲ

after: Burmese names the hour that has **already passed**, then adds "half": နှစ်နာရီခွဲ literally means "two o'clock, half". German *halb drei* and Indonesian *setengah tiga* name the hour **to come** — halfway to three.

The safe way to remember: **the number you hear is the hour that has passed.** If you hear သုံး, add thirty minutes to three o'clock. Exactly like English *half past three* — and like British "half three".

grammars.title: Morning, midday, evening, night — and where they go
body: Burmese divides the day into four parts, and the part of the day always comes **before** the clock time — the opposite of English "seven in the morning".

head: Burmese
Say it
Part of the day
Example
rows: မနက် ခုနစ်နာရီ — 7 a.m.
နေ့လယ် တစ်နာရီ — 1 p.m.
ညနေ ငါးနာရီ — 5 p.m.
ည ရှစ်နာရီ — 8 p.m.

after: ⚠️ We say "seven in the morning"; Burmese says မနက် ခုနစ်နာရီ — "morning seven o'clock". The pattern again: **the big unit first, the small one after**, just like the place expressions in unit 7.

grammars.title: Days and making appointments
body: Like the English days (Sunday, Monday, Saturday), the Burmese days are named after the sun, the moon, and the planets — here through Sanskrit astrology. နေ့ (*nay.*) at the end means "day".

head: Day
Burmese
Say it
rows: တနင်္လာနေ့
ဗုဒ္ဓဟူးနေ့
ကြာသပတေးနေ့
တနင်္ဂနွေနေ့

after: To make an appointment, the most common pattern is **time — place — တွေ့မယ်**: သုံးနာရီ ဘူတာရှေ့မှာ တွေ့မယ် (see you at three in front of the station). Notice that time comes before place, and the verb stays at the end.

blocks.text: These time expressions round out what you met in unit 8. They all go at the front of the sentence, and none of them changes the verb.

English

blocks.title: ⚠️ Myanmar's clock is thirty minutes off from its neighbors
items: Myanmar's time zone is **UTC+6:30** — half an hour behind Thailand and an hour and a half behind Singapore. Foreigners rarely remember the half hour, and it often wrecks appointments made by phone.
So when you arrange a call with someone abroad, state the time zone clearly. Ten in the morning in Yangon is 10:30 in Bangkok and 11:30 in Singapore.

For official and religious matters, people in Myanmar still use their own **lunar calendar**; the Burmese year is about 638 years behind the Western one. The full-moon day of each month, လပြည့်နေ့ (*la.-pyè.-nay.*), is a religious holiday, and many offices close.
